newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open to listless trading activity.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open to listless trading activity.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices opened quietly on Wednesday morning, still retaining a positive tone.
The focus of attention was expected to be on the Treasury's sale of five-year inflation-indexed securities, but the auction was not seen as having much influence on overall market sentiment.

May wholesale inventories were scheduled for release at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. Economists surveyed by Reuters expected that, on average, inventories would rise by 0.2 percent following a 0.7 percent decline the prior month.

Michelle Laughlin, economist with Prudential Securities Inc, said it was difficult to sell inflation-indexed securities in an environment without inflation and little generally expected in the near future.
"It has no liquidity because no one knows how to hedge them. Everyone's wondering who's going to buy them," said Laughlin.

But since TIPS issues have underperformed, they may draw some interest from investors who are not so confident inflation will remain contained, she said. Pension funds and insurance companies also will buy as a hedge, she said.
However, Laughlin expected the bond market to remain in current ranges regardless of how the auction went.

"We may be temporarily distracted by the claims number (on Thursday), but the event of the week is the Producer Price Index," Laughlin said. Even that was expected to be benign and the market would focus on the slew of data due next week, she said.
Market participants also would begin to speculate about Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upcoming Humphrey-Hawkins testimony. Greenspan is scheduled to testify before Congress on July 22.
After opening virtually unchanged, prices managed some gains.
Economists said the redemption of agency securities was one factor. Also nervousness about increased prepayment risk among mortgage-backed securities investors was prompting swaps into Treasuries.
The Treasury's 30-year bond was trading up 9/32 at 100-27/32 to yield 6.56 percent.
At the short end three-month bills were down two basis points at 4.95 percent. Six-month and year bills were down one basis point at 5.07 percent and 5.23 percent, respectively.
Ten-year issues were up 5/32 at 102-24/32, yielding 6.25 percent. Five years were up 3/32 at 100-14/32 to yield 6.15 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 at 100-6/32 to yield 5.90 percent.
(( John P. Hughes, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1663 ))
